source.title: Finding features in Transformers: Contrastive directions elicit stronger low-level perturbation responses than baselines

page_placements.theme: SAE feature directions as steering and causal handles (mixed)

record.tranche_reason: The post measures downstream responses to perturbations along SAE, contrastive, and random directions. It does not test SAE dictionary-size splitting, whether split features partition inputs, feature-family geometry, absorption, or the role of the sparsity objective.
record.gate_note: The reported perturbation-response comparisons are related to SAE features but do not measure any of the claim versions. They are recorded under fits_no_version, not as tests of splitting.
record.test_reason: The post compares downstream perturbation responses along contrastive, SAE-feature and random directions. It does not vary dictionary size or examine split features, feature families, absorption, cross-size decomposition, or training objectives. Its finding that SAE directions behave like random directions bears on SAE features in general, not on feature splitting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors also present the perturbation response as a candidate data-independent test for whether a direction is a feature. They say their SAE result confirms Lee & Heimersheim (2024) and Giglemiani et al. (2024).
record.recipe_differences: The study compares activation perturbations along contrastive, SAE-feature, and random directions; it does not use a feature-splitting method.
record.method_sensitivity: Perturbing at layer 2 produces stronger plateaus than at layer 8, although the contrastive-versus-other-directions difference remains clear. The text also reports consistent patterns with additive perturbations and alternative downstream metrics.

fits_no_version.finding: In Gemma 2-9B, Llama 3.1-8B and Qwen 3-1.7B, contrastive difference-of-means directions break through the activation plateau at smaller perturbation angles than SAE-feature or random directions. SAE-feature responses look similar to random directions in most cases. The post reports results as figures only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature directions are not treated specially by the model under perturbation; they respond like random directions, unlike contrastive directions.

record.problems: The post describes the results as preliminary. It uses ten held-out prompts per contrastive class, gives qualitative descriptions rather than numerical curve values in the text, and reports experiments at early layers with only a later-layer check for Gemma 2-9B.

untested.parts: all; SAEs used only as direction sources
all; the post's dataset-dependence point is cited, not tested

record.verdict_notes: Rows r1–r5 are correctly linked to none. Robustness checks (additive perturbation, KL and cosine metrics, layer 8) are summarised in method_sensitivity rather than recorded as separate rows, which is acceptable since none bears on any version. The author's comment reports about 80% Mandarin output tokens at about 20 degrees in Qwen3; this is off-claim.

relation.reason: It discusses whether SAE directions are the model's own features, which is related to the topic, but it never addresses splitting or tests any version.

tranche.reason: The post compares perturbation responses along contrastive, SAE and random directions. It does not vary dictionary size or look at split features, families, absorption or objectives, so it neither tests nor uses feature splitting.

source_check.notes: The rows are figure-only, with no numeric values. Qwen 3-1.7B is perturbed at layer 7; Gemma and Llama at layer 2. The study compares against random (FineWeb activation-difference) and SAE directions. The rows' baseline, 'unperturbed activations', is only the reference point for the L2 metric. Its finding that SAE directions get no special treatment is general evidence about SAE features, not about splitting.
